title: xWhy: Causal Interactive Learning
claim: Data alone leaves a class of indistinguishable models; explanations carve out a second class, and their intersection pinpoints the true model.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, Venn-like ellipses overlapping into a purple intersection
description: Three rounded beige panels, each labeled 'Model Space' and read left to right. The left panel, 'Observational Discovery' with a database icon, shows a blue ellipse containing four small five-node causal graphs (A–E). It is labeled MEC (Markov Equivalence Class) and captioned 'Models indistinguishable by data'. The middle panel, 'Explanatory Constraints' with a lightbulb icon, shows a red ellipse of five-node graphs, labeled EEC (Explanatory Equivalence Class). The graphs share the highlighted edge B→C, with the caption 'Models satisfying explanations, e.g., here'. The right panel, 'xWhyL', overlaps the blue and red ellipses. The purple intersection holds one dotted-circled graph, labeled 'Ground Truth Graph'. The eye goes first to the purple overlap in the rightmost panel. Blue, red and purple carry the logic.
caption: Illustrative Summary of our Contributions. We define \xwhyl as the search for a causal model that agrees with both data (MEC) and the provided explanations. To do so, we formalize the connection between causality and explanations, and show how explanations identify the Explanatory Equivalence Class (\eec) as the set of causal models agreeing with the given explanations. Ultimately, our goal is to converge towards the intersection of \mec and \eec. (Best viewed in color.)
abstract: Explanations are central to causal reasoning, and cognitive science has long established that the human drive to explain is itself a mechanism for learning about causality. Despite this, learning from those abductive signals is largely ignored in artificial intelligence. While explainable AI (XAI) increasingly draws on causal models to generate explanations, the converse direction about what explanations can do for causality remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we propose xWhyL, a formal framework connecting causality and XAI by learning causal models from explanations. We develop a mathematical theory that translates explanations into a learning signal complementary to observational data, and demonstrate how it enables overcoming the limits of observational causal discovery. As explanations can be derived from incorrect beliefs and clash with data, a tension we call the Causal Tug-of-War , we prove conditions under which our framework rejects misspecified explanations rather than absorbing them. Our practical instantiation, Causal Interactive Learning (CIL), shows how expert explanations can efficiently support causal discovery and distinguish correct from incorrect explanations.
